transcript:
This is NPR News Now, the latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Lyndi Kenyon.
South Dakota Republican Senator Mike Brown says new restrictions on Canada,
circulated by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth,
will not affect military operations, NATO, or intelligence sharing.
So what does it affect?
They're basically limiting some social engagements,
and they're asking people to get permission before they come in
and do think tanks and so forth, which is near as we can tell
is exactly the way that they've been operating for literally months already.
Virginia Democratic Senator Tim Kaine called the tone
of the administration's memo "bad and unnecessary,"
and he said the new Congress will change the tone dramatically.
The Trump administration had already banned Pentagon officials
from attending the Halifax International Security Forum
under restrictions imposed in 2025 on participating in think tanks.
The gathering usually draws about 300 military officials,
U.S. lawmakers, diplomats, and scholars annually.
Previous administrations of both parties sent senior Pentagon officials,
including Defense Secretaries.
Officials in the South East San Francisco Bay Area
are preparing for incredibly high king tides.
After being deluged with El Nino-fueled rains this week,
Brian Crownes reports from member station KQED.
Some residents have already begun preparing for the worst.
In a muddy parking lot near the Bay Shore,
Joseph Abu-Halawa filled up large white plastic bags with sand
and loaded them into the back of his pickup.
Definitely this year is probably the worst it's ever been.
Recent historic rainfall flooded his house in downtown Tiburon,
and Abu-Halawa isn't sure the sandbags can hold off the king tides.
I don't know, honestly.
I'm just doing it to make myself feel better,
because the damage is already pretty bad.
But it's going to make me feel at least more comfortable,
like I'm doing something about the problem.
The king tides are forecast to last three days,
peaking Wednesday at seven feet high.
For NPR News, I'm Brian Crownes.
A mathematician at Anthropics says he may have solved
what's being called the holy grail of math problems
with help from the company's chatbot, Claude.
NPR's Windsor Johnston reports the Riemann hypothesis
has been an open question for more than 160 years.
Rutgers University mathematician Alex Contruvitch says
he never expected to see a proof of the Riemann hypothesis in his lifetime.
I thought I was done picking myself up off the floor,
and I'm shocked, and I'm still shocked.
The hypothesis describes how prime numbers are spread out,
and getting to a solution means drawing on decades of work
across different branches of mathematics.
The new claim involves just massive, massive amounts of mathematics.
There's no human being that has all of that in their head.
Teams of human mathematicians will now examine parts of the computer code
and piece together how the proof works.
Contruvitch says understanding the proposed proof from Anthropics could take months.
You're listening to NPR.
A new effort is underway in northern Minnesota to help bring back an ancient fish.
Minnesota Public Radio's Dan Kroger reports on the giant lake sturgeon.
Sturgeon are enormous fish that can live well over 100 years.
They were wiped out from the St. Louis River in the mid-1900s.
For decades, biologists have worked to bring them back.
Miranda Rini with the Great Lakes Aquarium says this new approach
raises baby sturgeon directly in water from the river.
The sturgeon imprint on the water they're raised on
within the first 30 to 45 days of their life,
and that cues them of where to return to spawn.
Earlier this month, hundreds of seven-inch-long sturgeon were released into the river.
Have a good life, little buddies.
The goal is to make their populations self-sustaining.
For NPR News, I'm Dan Kroger in Duluth.
Well, this is a feat for anyone.
Deirdre Keen, a 38-year-old nurse practitioner and management consultant,
has completed all seven world marathon majors.
But here's the added hurdle.
She did it while pregnant with her first child.
After discovering she was pregnant following the Boston and London marathons,
Keen decided to continue pursuing her goal with approval from her doctor.
She ran her first marathon to honor her father, who was an avid runner,
who passed away from cancer when Keen was just 13 years old.
Keen said that running also helped her cope with the emotional challenges
of working in healthcare, especially the added complications that were posed
by the COVID-19 pandemic.
I'm Linda Kenyon, NPR News in Washington.

topics.text: Sen. Mike Brown says Hegseth's new Canada restrictions won't affect military operations, NATO, or intelligence
Sen. Tim Kaine calls Pentagon memo on Canada restrictions bad and unnecessary
San Francisco Bay Area officials prepare sandbags as record king tides approach, with Tiburon resident Joseph Abu-Halawa
Anthropic mathematician Alex Kontorovich says Claude helped crack the Riemann hypothesis, still being verified
Minnesota effort to restore lake sturgeon in St. Louis River using hatchery-raised fish released near Duluth
Nurse practitioner Deirdre Keen completes all seven World Marathon Majors while pregnant with first child
